6.caption: The green tile's every edge borders the other orbit. On the other tile, edges of the SAME colour are the ones they actually share; edges in a DIFFERENT colour border a same-orbit neighbour instead, so the perimeters can never be made equal. The two highlighted tiles do not share an edge or vertex.
6.note: Orbit A (3-gon) every edge cross-orbit (green). Orbit B (6-gon): 3 cross edges (green, matching A) + 3 self edges (orange, bordering another orbit-B tile) -- B always has extra perimeter A cannot supply.
6.reason: k = q with r >= k: every edge of the k-gon is cross-orbit, which forces the n-gon's self-edges to have total length (1 - r/k) * P <= 0. Perimeters cannot match, so one shape cannot serve both orbits.

31.caption: The shape in green is required for one orbit. The other orbit is restricted to the pink shaded region. This is impossible to fit in.
31.note: Proven impossible: orbifold pins the configuration and region to fixed (cone) points, so a single failed fit settles every member of the deformation family.
31.reason: Containment (netshape.html): orbit 1 is forced to contain a set of points pinned by the orbifold (each fixed by a rotation, or by two crossing mirrors), and orbit 2 is confined to the Voronoi cell of its own tile centre, whose corners are pinned the same way. The configuration admits no isometry into that region. Because the orbifold (*333/*442/*632) has a triangular fundamental domain with all angles fixed by its branching numbers, these points cannot move anywhere in the deformation family, so the single failed fit settles every member of the family. 90.caption: The shape in green is required for one orbit. The other orbit is restricted to the pink shaded region. This is impossible to fit in.
90.note: Orbit 2's tile carries a genuine 3-fold rotation, so monohedrality forces orbit 1's tile to be 3-fold symmetric as a shape. Its three forced points form an equilateral triangle T that exactly matches the kite region's three allowed corners; the only 3-fold centre keeping the rotated copy inside the kite is T's own centroid, and intersecting the kite with its two rotations leaves exactly T. So orbit 1 would have to be a straight-edged equilateral triangle -- but it is a 5-gon, so an edge (Config 2, 0.910684) collapses to zero. John's argument, verified numerically 2026-08-16.
90.reason: Containment (netshape.html, 'rotation-forces-shape' argument -- a NEW class, distinct from radius/rigid-orbifold): orbit 2's tile is a 3-gon whose centre carries a genuine 3-fold rotation (verified: rotation order exactly 3). Under the monohedral hypothesis orbit 1's tile is congruent to it, so orbit 1's tile must have 3-fold symmetry AS A SHAPE about some point O -- this need NOT be, and here is not, a symmetry of the tiling itself, so no group element sits at O.
